turn_text: You know, thank you for asking me that question because I get that question a lot from young people. And the first thing I say is I would not suggest that you try to enter politics as I did, losing in 76, losing in 78, and then losing and then winning again. If you're interested in politics and you're a young person, the thing I think you should do is to find some political person, candidate, office holder, that you have respect for and whose values you agree with and deeply engage yourself in that person's campaign. Because there's no way to learn politics like working in a political campaign. You can read about it in books, but unless you get in there and do the grubby work, make the phone calls, do all of that, those things that you've got to do in a campaign. You can't really understand what a campaign is like, and some people just don't like that kind of experience. Others feed upon it and love it and get excited about it and so on and so forth. Get involved in a campaign and figure out whether or not it's the kind of experience that brings meaning to your life. And if you dread it, if you don't look forward to getting up every day and going to work in the battlefield, then for God's sake, don't become a candidate.

turn_text: Well, it's very emotional, as a matter of fact. I mean, I'm 81 years old now. And I've done a lot of things in my life. I've been a United Methodist minister. I've been a college professor. I've worked in child care. I've been a congressman, I've been a governor, and I've been a family member, a husband, and a friend to a lot of people. And so I've been sort of going back over my life and trying to recall and to write what I remember. And it can be very emotional. It can be really emotional. But it's a good experience. It's good to remember people. And people have been so good to me across my political life as well as my personal life. And I'm trying to remember those people and those experiences and those relationships. I think I've settled on a title, a purposeful life, and the subtitle would be from living in a chicken shack to living in the governor's mansion. Because when I was a kid, I came from a family that was struggling a lot economically, and when I was about five years old, our home burned. And there were still nine of us kids. And we had nothing except we had a chicken shack that was built on the side of the hill. And we had what we called a smoke house that was at the bottom of the hill. And so my older brothers and my father went to work and they used cardboard for a wall board and they They put a wood floor in that chicken shack and we got beds from the Salvation Army. And so for a few months, our family lived in a chicken shack and we ate in the smokehouse. And I went to a one-room school until I was in fourth grade. And out of nine kids, only two of us finished high school. And I was able to go to college and get two master's degrees and a PhD degree and eventually be a congressman and a governor. And there are a lot of reasons why that was possible. But it was because of the people who loved me and cared for me and helped me. And I'm trying to write about those people and those experiences.
